articles.title: After bushfires hit their home, an Australian couple assembled 800 used laptop batteries into a 44-kWh solar battery; it helped them move toward off-grid living
articles.summary: Discover how an Australian couple transformed their lives by creating a sustainable off-grid home using solar energy and recycled laptop batteries after facing bushfires.
articles.body: In recent years, scorching bushfires have affected many people all over the world. In early 2020, during Australia's Black Summer bushfires, a couple from Wamboin, Syd Crawford and Camille Goodman, experienced this firsthand when bushfires threatened their home. After a close call at their property, the pair decided to change their way of life. Driven by the reality of climate change, they took some bold steps to reduce their carbon footprint.In an interview with ABC News, Dr Goodman explained that the couple recognized climate change as the major problem and began looking for practical things to take control and do their bit to save the environment. Trying to calculate an appropriate amount of emissions led them to pursue a zero-carbon lifestyle. The pair were aiming for their carbon footprint to be as close to zero as possible.Going off-grid using solar panels and recycled laptop batteriesTo cut their household emissions, Crawford and Goodman installed solar panels at their property. Thanks to these solar panels and a DIY storage system made from recycled laptop batteries, their home now operates almost entirely off the grid. In order to build the system, Crawford purchased laptop batteries by the kilo, then cracked them all open, tested the cells, and removed the defective ones. Laptop batteries often contain six cells; sometimes one cell is faulty, while the remaining five are fine, or all of them are in good condition. As cited by ABC News Australia, Crawford used 800 laptop batteries to build one big, substantial unit for a rooftop solar system. It offered a storage capacity of 44 kWh, roughly equivalent to three Tesla Powerwalls.Switching to electric vehicles to reduce carbon emissionsEven before the bushfires hit in early 2020, Crawford had tracked his emissions, establishing a 2019 baseline of just over 10 tonnes with three-quarters coming from his vehicles. Switching to electric cars made the biggest difference to his footprint. While he had always been environmentally conscious, he admitted that the idea of long car trips being a problem had never crossed his mind.According to the records, the pair tracked their individual emissions every year. In 2020, Crawford's total footprint dropped to 4.78 tonnes, with vehicle emissions falling to 1.8 tonnes. By 2022, his overall emissions decreased to 2.26 tonnes, and his vehicle emissions dropped to 0.85 tonnes.Overcoming the big hurdles for a carbon-zero lifestyleHowever, adopting a carbon-zero lifestyle came with its own challenges for the couple, especially as they got closer to their goal. Although the pair reduced their carbon emissions in 2021 by making simpler changes, further cuts became harder over time. Not only did they install solar panels and switch to electric appliances, but the pair also stopped flying and cut down on beef, lamb and dairy products.Around the same time, Goodman also began a job in Wollongong, a few hours’ drive from Wamboin, which meant that they had to quickly replace their newly purchased electric vehicles with ones that were capable of covering the longer distances. While these changes seemed a bit expensive at first, Goodman reflected that they ultimately improved the quality of their lives. When asked for advice on reducing emissions, she emphasised the importance of having realistic goals and simply doing your bit to save the environment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: A Wisconsin man has been charged with killing his marathon-running wife more than two years after she died in an alleged basement fall – with prosecutors pointing to texts about "powdery" water, an ominous Google search and a new girlfriend. Weeks earlier, on Sept. 18, 2024, Erica had confronted Carpenter over text about something in her drink, writing, "And what the f--- have you been doing to my water the past few days?!?!?" before adding, "There's been powdery s--- in it at least twice now." MISSOURI NURSE FOUND DEAD MONTHS AFTER ANESTHESIOLOGIST HUSBAND ADMITTED TO ASSAULTING WOMAN Instead, his actions immediately after Erica's death painted a far different picture. articles.title: A bronze cast of Auguste Rodin's The Thinker sold for $192,500 in 1985 and stayed off the market for 41 years; at a November 17 New York auction, the 1955 cast fetched $7.928 million, over twice its high estimate
articles.summary: The 1955 sculpture, officially titled Le Penseur, taille de la porte dit \"moyen modèle\", was sold at auction on Tuesday 17 November during Christie's 20th
articles.body: The 1955 sculpture, officially titled Le Penseur, taille de la porte dit "moyen modèle", was sold at auction on Tuesday 17 November during Christie's 20th Century Evening Sale. Christie's auction records show that the sculpture had an estimated price of $2.5 million to $3.5 million before the sale, but strong bidding pushed the final price, including the buyer's premium, to $7,928,000. According to art market intelligence firm HENI, the sculpture was last sold at auction on 14 May 1985 at Sotheby's in New York. It was listed as lot 3 and sold for $192,500. HENI reported that the latest sale price was $7.74 million higher than the 1985 result. This represents an increase of 4,018 per cent and an average annual return of 9 per cent over four decades.Four decades in private handsChristie's sale records trace the sculpture's ownership back to its creation in Paris in 1955. The Musée Rodin was its first owner before New York dealer World House Galleries bought it in December that year. World House Galleries displayed the bronze in its Four Masters exhibition in spring 1957. After its sale at Sotheby's in May 1985, the sculpture remained in private hands for 41 years. It returned to auction this month as part of the William I. Koch Collection. The collection was one of six named collections featured during Christie's main 20th and 21st Century Art auction week at Rockefeller Center. Christie's did not reveal the identity of the winning bidder. The final sale price also does not include taxes or shipping costs.Origins of the door-sized castRodin's seated figure is best known today through much larger versions displayed in public gardens and museums. However, this 71.4-centimetre bronze keeps the sculpture's original proportions. Christie's catalogue notes state that Rodin first designed the figure in 1880 to sit at the top of La Porte de l'Enfer (The Gates of Hell). It represented a poet looking down at the scenes below. Rodin settled on the final design in 1882. He then separated the figure from the larger doorway and made it an independent sculpture in 1884. It was cast at the exact height it had occupied on the doorway. This size became known in French as taille de la porte, or moyen modèle. According to Musée Rodin records cited in Christie's sale notes, 17 bronze versions of this size were made during Rodin's lifetime. Another 17 were produced between 1919 and 1945, followed by a final group of nine casts between 1954 and 1969.The 1955 sculpture sold in New York belongs to this final group of nine. It was made by the Georges Rudier foundry in Paris using bronze with a dark brown and green finish. It measures 71.4 by 43.8 by 66.7 centimetres. Several marks on the bronze help confirm its identity. These include Rodin's signature on the right side of the rock, a raised signature underneath, the Georges Rudier foundry stamp on the back and the inscription "© by Musee Rodin 1955" on the left side. The Comité Rodin has also registered the sculpture under archive number 2021-6376B for its upcoming catalogue critique.Strong demand during New York marquee weekThe Rodin sculpture was sold during a strong opening night for Christie's November auction series in New York. Christie's reported that its 20th Century Evening Sale on 17 November brought in $626,621,400. A total of 92 per cent of the lots sold, while 95 per cent of the works sold by value. Sculptures attracted strong bids throughout the evening. An Alberto Giacometti bronze made around 1949, Figure, demie grandeur (no. 2), sold for $25,980,000. The work came from the collection of Herbert Lust and was offered without a minimum sale price. Works by Joan Miró and Fernando Botero also set new auction records for sculptures by those artists.The highest price of the evening went to Wassily Kandinsky's 1922-1923 painting Betonte Ecken. It sold for $85,780,000 and set an auction record for the artist. Gustav Klimt's 1915-1916 landscape Litzlbergkeller followed at $82,330,000, while Claude Monet's Champ d'avoine et coquelicots sold for $25,980,000. Across all its 20th and 21st Century Art sales in New York that week, Christie's recorded total sales of $973,978,632. For the 1955 Le Penseur, the $7.928 million sale ended a 41-year gap between its public auction appearances. The result also placed the mid-century bronze well above its estimated price before the sale.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Huang in there! Trump's bra-zen tribute to tech bro he rescued
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: MAGA boss Donald Trump has never been one to let conventional presidential decorum get in the way of a provocative
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: MAGA boss Donald Trump has never been one to let conventional presidential decorum get in the way of a provocative social-media stunt. So when Nvidia chief Jensen Huang returned to his corporate throne after an extra-marital affairs scandal, the US President, himself a seasoned veteran in this sphere, celebrated it by posting a meme of Huang waving a red bra in place of a clenched fist he (Trump) had raised after surviving an assassination attempt.Trump was apparently having a laugh, but not everyone was amused. On CNN, Scott Jennings, the conservative commentator and Trump defender, was challenged by guest host Elie Honig to explain the image. Told to lighten up and that it was just a joke, Honig reminded him of Cory Comperatore, the man who lost his life during the assassination attempt and asked, "Do you think his family is laughing?"For critics, the issue is not so much about Trump's bizarre sense of humour, but that the office of the presidency has become a social-media trolling operation. One angry reaction captured the sentiment with copulatory nouns and verbs, accusing Trump of having "degraded and debased the institution of the presidency" and lamenting a political culture in which billionaire interests seemed to matter more than public standards.Others questioned what message the President was sending about fidelity and accountability. Here was a man with his own long and well-documented history of marital infidelity and sex scandals, making light of another powerful man's extramarital relationships. The objection was not necessarily that Huang should be denied a second chance. It was the apparent double standard: personal conduct that might have serious consequences for ordinary employees or executives was being transformed into a badge of masculine resilience when the person involved was sufficiently powerful, wealthy or strategically useful.There was, meanwhile, another curious dimension to Trump's defence of Huang. Having pronounced him a patriot and a national asset, the president introduced an ethnic qualification that was distinctly less reassuring. Huang was born in Taiwan, and Trump suggested that, had Washington failed to bring him back, China might have recruited him to lead Huawei's AI operations. "He's got a little Chinese blood in him," Trump said, suggesting that if Huang had been treated badly, he might have been tempted by an offer from Beijing. It was an extraordinary observation, not least because it appeared to conflate ethnicity with national allegiance.The controversy also exposed a more consequential contradiction within Trump's own camp. Several Republican lawmakers have questioned both Huang's reinstatement and the administration's intervention. Senators including Tom Cotton and Pete Ricketts have insisted that the company's national-security questions remain unresolved and that Huang must still answer congressional inquiries. The concerns relate not simply to his personal relationships but to possible exposure of sensitive American semiconductor technology to China.Trump, however, has shown little inclination to follow the Republican establishment's preferred script. On China, as with Russia, he has resisted the hawkish instincts of his own party. On immigration, tariffs, foreign policy and even the conduct of the federal government, he has repeatedly departed from conventional Republican positions, often demanding that his party fall in line behind him.The question increasingly being asked is not simply what Trump will do next, but what, if anything, constitutes a red line for him and for the Republican Party that has largely accommodated his instincts. If a president can personally lobby for the reinstatement of a billionaire executive facing national-security questions, dismiss the surrounding scandal as potentially good publicity and then celebrate the outcome with a lingerie meme built around an assassination attempt, what exactly is beyond the pale?For Trump, perhaps nothing is. Every controversy is an opportunity, every outrage an audience, and every institutional convention another obstacle to be trampled, preferably with a camera rolling. The Huang affair is particularly revealing because Trump has managed to combine several presidential roles in a single episode: corporate dealmaker, national-security arbiter, moral relativist, ethnic commentator, and internet comedian. He has intervened in and influenced a private company's boardroom decision, vouched for an executive facing serious questions, and then turned the executive's sexual scandal into a piece of presidential entertainment. Even his most trenchant critics admit this: No one, absolutely no one, could have done this.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two millionaire couples in London's Primrose Hill have spent six years fighting over a concrete wall allegedly extending 900mm into a neighbour's property, with £100,000 in compensation at stake
articles.summary: Two millionaire couples in Primrose Hill, north London, are locked in a six-year legal dispute over a concrete basement wall that allegedly bulges up to
articles.body: Two millionaire couples in Primrose Hill, north London, are locked in a six-year legal dispute over a concrete basement wall that allegedly bulges up to 900mm onto a neighbouring property. Safina Haleema and Anthony O'Connor are demanding £100,000 in compensation from Amy McKeown and Matthew Dalton, who deny trespass and cite a 2016 party wall agreement. The dispute has reportedly racked up £160,000 in legal costs. At a pre-trial hearing, Judge Nicholas Parfitt declined to strike out the claim, giving the claimants a final chance to set out their case in definitive particulars.How did a basement project spark a six-year legal battleThe Independent reports that Philip Jones, barrister for Mr O'Connor and Ms Haleema, told the court the conflict stemmed from basement works carried out ten years ago. He said these ended in a concrete "overspill" that caused the neighbours' wall to bulge out beneath the claimants' home. Mr Jones described the case as relatively straightforward and said the central question was whether Mr Dalton and Ms McKeown, through their contractors, caused or permitted concrete to be poured so that it protruded up to 900mm onto the claimants' land and into what is now their basement.Mr O'Connor and Ms Haleema say they discovered the underground overspill after commissioning their own basement dig in 2020, although they later abandoned the project. Mr Jones disputed any suggestion that his clients' case lacked clarity. He argued that, whatever the extent of the permitted works, the defendants "hugely exceeded it" and encroached significantly onto the claimants' land, causing damage.Why do the neighbours deny the £100,000 compensation claimThe report says Ms McKeown, an award-winning mental health and wellbeing consultant for businesswomen, and Mr Dalton deny that their wall trespasses over the boundary line. They are also contesting their neighbours' bid for a court ruling on the precise location of the boundary and the claim for £100,000 in compensation. Their barrister, Hugh Rowan, called the claim "absurd". He said his clients had been stuck in limbo for six years and could not sell their house or move away, because doing so would reveal the existence of the dispute.According to The Independent, Mr Rowan pointed to a party wall agreement made between the neighbours in 2016, which he said made clear the new basement wall was permitted to straddle the boundary. He said the claimants' own expert accepted that the 2016 award allowed a retaining wall astride the party wall boundary. He also argued that any compensation would amount to "double recovery", because Mr O'Connor and Ms Haleema had previously received an insurance payout for the concrete overspill in 2023. His name once appeared as "Mr O'Connell", apparently a typographical slip, but otherwise refers to Mr O'Connor.Why did the millionaire neighbours' basement wall dispute return to courtThe Independent reports that the case reached court for a pre-trial hearing. Ms McKeown and Mr Dalton asked Judge Nicholas Parfitt to strike out the claim, which they described as hopeless, on the grounds of lack of clarity and inconsistency. Mr Rowan argued that the claimants' pleadings were full of inconsistencies, contradictions and speculation. He noted that their original claim said the neighbours' wall should have stopped at the boundary line, which he said contradicted the 2016 agreement. He added that the claim was later revised to say the wall needed to be straight rather than display an overspill of concrete. By his account, the claimants had still not clarified where the alleged overspill begins, how much overspill is alleged or what the cost of a remedy would be.The judge declined to dismiss the case after several hours of argument. He instead gave Mr O'Connor and Ms Haleema a final chance to prepare definitive particulars of claim setting out the details of their legal case. The report says the case is due to return to court at a later date. The Independent also notes that the area is a sought-after address, associated with past and present celebrities such as Daniel Craig, Jamie Oliver and Harry Styles, and with Jude Law's "Primrose Hill Set" of the 1990s.Disclaimer: This article is based on a report published by The Independent and on information available in the public domain. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the legal dispute, the allegations, the financial figures (including the compensation sought and the legal costs mentioned) or the circumstances of the property works. The claims made by the claimants are allegations and are denied by the defendants. The case is ongoing, and no final judgment has been delivered on its merits. The information should not be interpreted as confirmation or comment from any of the individuals named, or from their representatives or legal counsel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Six Tribal Nations file federal lawsuits against Trump administration over renewed attempts to revoke protections for sacred Utah monuments Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante
articles.summary: For generations, the canyons, mesas and ancient landmarks of Utah have held deep cultural and spiritual meaning for Native American communities.
articles.body: For generations, the canyons, mesas and ancient landmarks of Utah have held deep cultural and spiritual meaning for Native American communities. They are not just stretches of protected wilderness but places where ancestors lived, ceremonies were performed, medicines were gathered and traditions were passed down.Now, six Tribal Nations are taking their fight to court to protect these ancestral lands after US President Donald Trump renewed efforts to revoke protections for two major national monuments in Utah.The Tribal Nations have filed two federal lawsuits challenging the administration's latest actions concerning Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments. They argue that the moves violate federal law, undermine Tribal sovereignty and threaten places that remain central to their identities.According to Native News Online, the lawsuits were filed on November 18, 2026, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. The Native American Rights Fund (NARF) brought the cases on behalf of the six Tribal Nations.Why six Tribal Nations have taken the fight to courtThe legal challenge is divided into two cases, each focusing on one of the national monuments.The first lawsuit has been filed on behalf of the Pueblo of Zuni, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe and Hopi Tribe. It challenges Trump's latest attempt to revoke protections for Bears Ears National Monument. It also questions the administration's reported move to dismantle the Bears Ears Commission, a body that gives Tribal Nations a formal role in decisions concerning the monument's stewardship.The second lawsuit represents the Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians, Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah and Ute Mountain Ute Tribe. It challenges the administration's attempt to revoke protections for Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.Together, the two cases seek to protect more than two million acres of land that the Tribal Nations consider sacred and essential to their histories, cultures and religious practices.'These lands are an unbroken record of who we are'For the Pueblo of Zuni, Bears Ears is far more than a landscape of striking rock formations and canyons. It holds the physical traces of generations who came before them.Zuni Head Councilman Anthony Sanchez explained the deep connection his people share with the monument, pointing to its ancestral dwellings, ceremonial sites, burial grounds and gathering places.“Bears Ears’ canyons and mesas hold the dwellings, ceremonial sites, burial grounds, and gathering places of our ancestors,” Sanchez said. “These lands are an unbroken record of who we are and where we come from. It is our sovereign right as Tribal Nations to steward this land for generations to come.”Hopi Tribe Vice Chairman Mikah Kewanimptewa also stressed that the importance of Bears Ears cannot be measured by its scenic beauty alone. The landscape contains ancestral rock markings, artefacts and landmarks that preserve the history of his people.“Bears Ears National Monument is more than a scenic backdrop,” Kewanimptewa said. “Our history is inextricably woven into the landscape, recorded in ancestral rock markings, artifacts, and landmarks. These are sacred lands, not exploration sites for mining and extraction.”Why Grand Staircase-Escalante matters to Native American communitiesThe concerns extend beyond Bears Ears. Grand Staircase-Escalante also holds generations of cultural and religious connections for Native communities.For the Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians, the area contains traditional medicines, cultural resources and places connected to their history. Chairman Roland Maldonado said protecting the monument was tied to the responsibility of preserving these resources for future generations.“These sacred lands hold our plant medicines, cultural resources, and histories that Tribal Nations are required to protect for the next generation,” Maldonado said. “Grand Staircase is inseparable from our culture, history, and identity, and we will continue to defend Tribal lands and protect the integral cultural resources within Grand Staircase-Escalante.”Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Chairwoman Laurel Yellowhorse also described the monument as a place where members of her community continue to practise their religious and cultural traditions.“Grand Staircase is a land like nowhere else for Paiute people,” Yellowhorse said. “It’s where our citizens travel to pray and to gather plants and medicines necessary for religious ceremonies. These are sacred lands, not potential mining sites.”What is behind the legal battle over the monuments?The dispute is rooted in the Antiquities Act of 1906, a federal law that allows US presidents to designate national monuments to protect historic landmarks, structures and other objects of historic or scientific interest.NARF argues that while the law gives presidents the authority to establish national monuments, it does not give them the power to revoke protections for monuments that have already been designated. The organisation maintains that such authority belongs to Congress.The lawsuits also challenge the administration's reported attempt to abolish the Bears Ears Tribal Commission and remove the federal government's obligation to consult the commission on the monument's management.NARF Deputy Director Matthew L. Campbell accused the administration of disregarding Tribal sovereignty and acting against federal law.“Once again, the Trump administration is trying to revoke these National Monuments, this time by disregarding Tribal sovereignty and again in violation of federal law,” Campbell said.He added that the Antiquities Act authorises presidents to declare national monuments but does not expressly give them the power to revoke existing ones. “The court should block implementation of these unlawful directives,” he said.The legal argument will now be placed before the federal court, which will be asked to intervene and prevent the administration from implementing the challenged actions.Trump had targeted the monuments in 2017 as wellThis is not the first time the two monuments have faced efforts to reduce or remove their protections.Trump attempted to scale back protections for Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante through presidential proclamations in 2017. His administration's latest actions in 2026 have brought the dispute back into the spotlight.The current lawsuits seek to challenge those renewed efforts and protect the Tribal Nations' role in decisions affecting their ancestral lands.For the communities involved, the issue goes beyond environmental conservation or government land-management policy. It concerns the protection of burial grounds, ceremonial sites, traditional medicines and cultural resources that connect present generations to their ancestors.The six Tribal Nations say they have lived on, travelled across and cared for these lands since time immemorial. Their legal battle is also about ensuring that future generations can continue to visit these places, practise their traditions and maintain their connection to their homelands.The Pueblo of Zuni is represented in the Bears Ears case by NARF along with the law firm Sonosky, Chambers, Sachse, Mielke & Brownell, LLP.The two lawsuits now seek judicial intervention to stop the administration's proposed actions and preserve protections for the monuments, as well as the Tribal stewardship arrangements associated with them.You use AI every day. articles.title: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.summary: Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly on...
articles.body:
Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.

Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia's statistical bureau, Rosstat.

But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets.

That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia's death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret.

Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat's servers earlier this month.

CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll.

Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents.

But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums.

By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000.

Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%.

The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates.

In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia's recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan.

Like Russia, Ukraine doesn't release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.

Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that the combined death toll suffered by Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million.

As the newly projected death toll underscores the human cost of Moscow's war, fears are growing in Ukraine over a deteriorating security situation in the country's eastern Donetsk region – an area mostly under Russian control – amid daily guided bomb and drone attacks .

All families with children still in Donetsk were on Tuesday ordered to evacuate.

Children and families in many communities in most of Ukrainian-controlled Donetsk - including the major cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - were already under the evacuation order, but now the measure has been expanded to settlements further west. An estimated 64,500 civilians remain in the region as of November 2026, according to the Donetsk regional military administration.

"This is an extremely difficult but necessary decision. The Russians are shelling our cities and villages every day and bombarding the region with aerial bombs," said the head of Donetsk's regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin.

For months, Moscow's forces have been inching towards Kramatorsk , one of Ukraine's last strongholds in the north of Donetsk region. Tuesday's mandatory evacuation order is a sign of Kyiv's concern that an expansion of Russian attacks could further harm civilians and isolate communities, for example by blowing up bridges and supply routes.

CNN's Clare Sebastian, Nathan Hodge, Kosta Gak and Lauren Kent contributed reporting.

articles.title: New York’s proposed horse-carriage ban has triggered a federal legal challenge after Mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani signed the measure; the case could determine the future of an iconic but controversial city tradition
articles.summary: New York City’s plan to end its horse-drawn carriage industry is facing an immediate legal challenge, with the union representing carriage drivers and
articles.body: New York City’s plan to end its horse-drawn carriage industry is facing an immediate legal challenge, with the union representing carriage drivers and owners taking the fight to federal court just minutes after Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the ban into law. According to reports by the Associated Press, NBC New York and Bloomberg Law, the lawsuit argues that the legislation threatens workers’ livelihoods and takes away valuable business assets without guaranteeing compensation. Filed on November 19 in Manhattan federal court, the proposed class-action lawsuit names the Transport Workers Union of America, TWU Local 100, a carriage licence owner and two drivers among the plaintiffs. It seeks to have the legislation declared unconstitutional and prevent the city from enforcing it.At the centre of the dispute is Romanch’s Law, which will bring New York City’s horse-drawn carriage operations to an end by June 1, 2028. The legislation also means existing carriage licences will expire on May 31, 2028, effectively ending an industry that has been part of the city’s identity for more than 160 years. The union’s legal challenge centres on the financial consequences for people who have invested in the business. City-issued carriage licences, commonly known as medallions, represent significant assets, with some owners having paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to secure them. The plaintiffs argue that eliminating these licences without guaranteed compensation amounts to an unconstitutional taking of private property. They have also raised concerns about the city’s legislative procedures and restrictions on transferring carriage horses to operators in places where the industry remains legal.The dispute comes as the Mamdani administration attempts to establish a transition programme for approximately 200 people whose livelihoods depend on the industry. A framework announced earlier this month includes plans to explore medallion buybacks, alongside employment assistance for drivers and stable workers.The administration intends to introduce a Horse Carriage Worker Industry Program in partnership with city agencies. It is expected to offer career counselling, professional training, educational opportunities, tuition assistance and connections with potential employers. A comprehensive transition plan is due by April 1, 2027, as required under the legislation. However, compensation for business owners has not been guaranteed and remains subject to further consideration by the city.The mayor’s office is also examining alternatives to traditional carriage rides, including electric carriages and electric pedal-assist bicycles, through a feasibility study. Meanwhile, the administration has indicated that it will work with animal rescue organisations and sanctuaries to arrange retirement options for the horses. Under the new law, carriage horses cannot be transferred for slaughter or continued use in another horse-drawn carriage business.The legislation gained momentum following the death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan, who lost his life in a carriage accident in Central Park on June 17, 2026. The incident renewed public scrutiny of the industry, particularly concerns surrounding passenger safety, unpredictable traffic conditions and the welfare of horses navigating increasingly crowded city streets. The law was subsequently named in his memory.On October 22, the New York City Council approved Romanch’s Law in a 40-7 vote, with Council Member Christopher Marte sponsoring the measure and Speaker Julie Menin supporting its passage. Animal welfare organisations have long campaigned to end the practice, arguing that the demands of operating horse-drawn carriages in a modern urban environment create risks that cannot be adequately addressed through regulation alone.However, industry representatives maintain that existing licensing requirements, veterinary inspections, working-hour restrictions and weather-related suspensions provide safeguards that allow the business to operate responsibly. They argue that the city should strengthen these measures rather than eliminate the industry altogether.The city’s Law Department has confirmed that it is reviewing the lawsuit. With the union seeking to block the legislation before its implementation deadline, the case could become a significant legal test of the city’s authority to phase out a longstanding commercial tradition while addressing the property and employment rights of those affected. For now, the June 2028 deadline remains in place, but the future of New York’s iconic horse-drawn carriages may ultimately depend on what the federal court decides.You use AI every day. articles.title: Colorado man Stephen Martinez, freed after 27 years when his murder conviction over an infant's death was overturned, is now seeking about $2 million from the state, and the baby's family calls his claim a joke
articles.summary: A Colorado man who spent 27 years in prison before his murder conviction over the death of a four-month-old girl was overturned has filed a claim seeking
articles.body: A Colorado man who spent 27 years in prison before his murder conviction over the death of a four-month-old girl was overturned has filed a claim seeking about $1.9 million in state compensation. The baby's family has strongly opposed the request, calling it "a joke". Stephen Martinez was released in April 2026 after a Denver judge overturned his 2000 first-degree murder conviction. According to The Denver Post, Martinez has now filed a petition under Colorado's wrongful conviction compensation law, seeking around $1.9 million for the years he spent behind bars. Denver publication Westword reported that relatives of the baby, Heather Mares, strongly object to the payment and have described Martinez's compensation claim as "a joke".Legal battle over actual innocenceUnder a Colorado law introduced in 2013, people who are wrongly convicted of a felony and later cleared can seek $70,000 for every year they spent in prison. They may also qualify for benefits such as healthcare and tuition waivers. Based on Martinez's 27 years in prison, the payment could come close to $2 million. However, having a conviction overturned does not mean someone automatically receives compensation. As Denver television station 9NEWS explained, Colorado's law requires people making a claim to prove in court that they are "actually innocent"."A court or a jury has to determine that there really was a miscarriage of justice and that they had no role at all – entire innocence – as it relates to the crime in question," 9NEWS legal analyst Scott Robinson said. Martinez's lawyers say new medical evidence supports his claim that he had no role in the baby's death. Attorney Jeanne Segil, assistant director of the Korey Wise Innocence Project at the University of Colorado Law School, told The Denver Post that the petition is based on updated medical findings."We are bringing this petition under the compensation statute because Stephen Martinez is actually innocent," Segil said. "What happened here was a tragedy, but it was not a crime. The medical experts in the case are all clear the baby died from natural causes. Stephen did not cause her death."The 1998 death and 2000 convictionThe case began on 17 November 1998, when Martinez called 911 from his home in Denver. He reported that four-month-old Heather Mares, the daughter of his then-girlfriend, was choking. According to accounts reported by The Denver Post, Martinez told paramedics that he had given the baby a bottle because she was crying. He said he then put her down and went into another room. A few minutes later, he heard her choking and returned to find her in distress. Emergency workers were unable to save her.Hospital examinations and later investigations found that Heather had a skull fracture, bleeding in her brain, swelling and burst blood vessels in her eyes. Prosecutors argued that these injuries showed she had been violently shaken. Martinez was convicted of first-degree murder in 2000. According to Law Week Colorado, Martinez was the first person sentenced under a Colorado law that made life in prison without the possibility of parole mandatory for the offence.Why the murder conviction was overturnedMartinez's conviction remained in place for more than 25 years. That changed after lawyers from the Korey Wise Innocence Project, working with pro bono attorneys from law firm Stinson LLP, independent counsel Seth Temin and volunteer law students, filed a petition to reopen the case. In April 2026, Denver District Attorney John Walsh agreed to overturn the conviction after reviewing updated medical evidence. The new findings suggested that the baby had died from severe pneumonia rather than abuse.At the time of Martinez's release, Walsh said the investigators and prosecutors involved in the original case had relied on the medical knowledge available to them in 2000. "This is simply an example of the criminal justice system being willing and able to reassess a case when necessary," Walsh said. Perry Glantz, a partner at Stinson LLP and a board member of the innocence project, criticised the beliefs behind the original prosecution in an interview with Law Week Colorado."What was wrong about Shaken Baby Syndrome was it was almost more of a belief system than a scientific reality," Glantz said. "They're like, well, he was the only one there. It has to be him. There was really no investigation."Release from prison and next stepsWhen Martinez left the Lindsey Flanigan Courthouse in Denver on 21 April 2026, relatives and his wife were waiting for him. He had married his wife while in prison. Both of his parents had died during the 27 years he spent serving his sentence. "I'm so happy and so thankful to be out after being locked up for 27 years, innocent," Martinez told CBS News outside the courthouse. "But now I'm going out to absolutely nothing. But God bless you, guys, have a great day."Martinez's compensation petition is now before the court. A judge must decide whether he meets Colorado's strict legal test for actual innocence before he can receive any money from the state. Having his murder conviction overturned was a major step, but the compensation claim requires a separate legal decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Hardest meeting of my life’: Jensen Huang apologises to Nvidia staff after CEO comeback
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologised to employees on Tuesday for violating the company's code of conduct and admitted making “very serious personal
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologised to employees on Tuesday for violating the company's code of conduct and admitted making “very serious personal mistakes” during his first all-hands meeting since returning to the top post. Huang acknowledged that his personal behaviour had hurt his family and wife. He also promised to hold himself to higher standards and undergo regular performance reviews based on feedback from employees.“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said, according to a report by The Wired. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”Huang says he is undergoing therapyAddressing employees, Huang said he had been attending therapy sessions every day for an hour and a half. He added that the sessions had been helping him.“I made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife,” he said.Huang also stressed that Nvidia's code of conduct remained applicable to everyone in the company, including its top leadership. He said he had written much of the code himself and that it was designed to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”He warned that violations would not be tolerated. However, he clarified that every violation would not automatically lead to an employee's dismissal.“But that does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would determine the action taken.Nvidia CEO promises regular performance reviewsHuang also addressed criticism of his intense management style and acknowledged that his behaviour had sometimes affected employees negatively.While he maintained that his demanding approach helped push people to perform better, he admitted that he sometimes went too far.“It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said.He said he needed to find a way to maintain his commitment to Nvidia without hurting the people working for him.“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” he said.Huang also announced that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review. The process would involve seeking feedback from people working with him, potentially as often as once a month.He said he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and did not intend to introduce the practice across the company.Huang rejects claims of preferential treatmentThe CEO also pushed back against suggestions that he had been reinstated because of his standing in the technology industry.“There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said.He rejected the suggestion that his position gave him special treatment or placed him above Nvidia's code of conduct.Huang also sought to reassure women employees, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women”.He highlighted the company's flexible work policies, saying they allowed employees to build their families while pursuing their careers.“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” he said.He further sought to reassure employees about the company's ability to function without him, saying his brief absence had demonstrated its operational strength.“I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.Why Huang stepped down and returned as Nvidia CEONvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation earlier this month following concerns about his personal conduct and lack of candour. The development came after media reports about alleged extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman accused of having links to Chinese intelligence services.However, the same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days after accepting his resignation. The decision followed fresh assurances from Huang and information from the Trump administration that he was not under federal scrutiny.His return has drawn mixed reactions within Nvidia. While some employees welcomed the decision, others reportedly remain concerned about his conduct and the board's move to reinstate him.The controversy has also led to continued legal and regulatory scrutiny. Nvidia's board is investigating whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence. US lawmakers are also expecting him to testify before Congress next week.Meanwhile, lawsuits and other investigations are ongoing into the company's disclosures about Huang's conduct and its compliance with US export controls on chips.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: A 5th-century boat burial on Germany’s North Sea coast reveals a man's Danube origins and a rare leprosy pathogen identified through DNA analysis, offering clues to ancient disease spread and human migration
articles.summary: A man buried in a boat grave on Germany’s North Sea coast during the 5th century came from the Danube region and carried an unusual form of leprosy, DNA
articles.body: A man buried in a boat grave on Germany’s North Sea coast during the 5th century came from the Danube region and carried an unusual form of leprosy, DNA analysis has found. The discovery came from the Fallward burial site, located in present-day Cuxhaven district.The pathogen belongs to a group whose earliest known representative was identified in ancient Egypt, but which had not previously been detected in Central or Northern Europe.According to Kiel University, the pathogen was identified while analysing bone samples from 11 people. The findings provide evidence of long-distance human movement and the spread of disease in Late Antiquity.How DNA analysis identified a rare leprosy pathogen in an ancient boat burialThe Fallward burial ground is located in the Cuxhaven district, along Germany’s North Sea coast. Archaeologists from the district’s heritage conservation department investigated the site in the 1990s. Damp soil had preserved wooden and textile objects in the graves. Researchers are analysing the finds through a project funded by the German Research Foundation at the NIhK in Wilhelmshaven.Objects recovered in blocks and kept frozen are being examined under laboratory conditions. The Ancient DNA Working Group at Kiel University’s Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology received bone samples from 11 individuals. The team aimed to investigate possible genetic relationships and look for traces of infectious diseases among those buried there.Researchers uncover unusual objects in ancient boat burialProfessor Ben Krause-Kyora, lead researcher at IKMB, said, “Three of the individuals provided sufficient data for a population genetic analysis. The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual.”Reportedly, the man had been buried in a boat along with numerous grave goods made of wood, pottery and metal.Professor Hauke Jöns of the NIhK said, “The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest; these included a chair, artfully decorated and carved from an alder trunk. Furthermore, the man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances.”The pathogen belongs to a group whose earliest known representative came from Egypt and dates to between the 4th and 2nd centuries BC.DNA analysis traces man's origins to the Danube regionProfessor Almut Nebel from the IKMB said, “Leprosy is a chronic disease. It can take years for clear symptoms to appear. The man had not yet suffered any bone damage. Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease.”Reportedly, the genetic analyses thus confirm the picture of a man who, although buried on the North Sea coast, had his roots in the Danube region and had connections to south-eastern Europe and the Mediterranean. He presumably lived there for a certain period of time.Professor Dr Ben Krause-Kyora said, “He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser. Or he might have undertaken long journeys as a trader.”What DNA revealed about the man's journey across EuropeThe analyses indicate that the man buried on the North Sea coast had roots in the Danube region and connections to south-eastern Europe and the Mediterranean. Researchers believe he probably lived in that wider region for some time, although his exact origins remain unknown. Professor Ben Krause-Kyora suggested he might have served as a mercenary in the Roman army before settling between the Elbe and Weser rivers.Another possibility is that he travelled long distances as a trader. The researchers said the findings show the complexity of individual lives during Late Antiquity. They also highlight how people and pathogens moved across far-reaching networks in a world connected over considerable distances.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 1,000 tonnes of shredded household and commercial waste dumped illegally in England town; investigation launched in West Yorkshire as hunt for those responsible begins
articles.summary: A huge mound of shredded household and commercial waste has appeared on a plot of land in Birstall, West Yorkshire, leaving investigators searching for
articles.body: A huge mound of shredded household and commercial waste has appeared on a plot of land in Birstall, West Yorkshire, leaving investigators searching for those responsible. The estimated 1,000 tonnes of rubbish, piled high near industrial and commercial premises, has triggered an investigation by England's Environment Agency.The waste, which includes shredded material flecked with plastic, was found on land off Bankwood Way. Environment Agency officers visited the site on November 4 following reports of the dumping. The agency announced the investigation on November 13 and has appealed to the public for information.Photographs released by the agency show large piles of waste reaching above the height of an officer standing nearby, with electricity pylons visible in the background. Despite the scale of the dumping, investigators have not yet identified who was responsible or established exactly when the waste was brought to the site.Police and council join investigation into illegal dumpingThe Environment Agency says it is pursuing several lines of enquiry to identify those behind the incident. The landowner has been cooperating with investigators to secure the site and prevent further waste from being dumped there.West Yorkshire Police and Kirklees Council are also assisting with the assessment and monitoring of the ground. Investigators have made enquiries with neighbouring businesses as they try to establish how the waste arrived and who was involved.Ben Hocking, Area Environment Manager at the Environment Agency, said illegal waste sites create problems for local communities and damage the environment.“Illegal waste sites cause misery for communities and are a blight on the environment,” he said.The agency has not disclosed the estimated cost of removing the waste or who will ultimately be responsible for the cleanup.Government warns waste criminals as fines set to increaseThe Birstall investigation comes as the government steps up its efforts to tackle illegal waste dumping across England.Waste Minister Emma Hardy said the government was increasing enforcement activity, including putting more officers on the frontline and using drones to identify illegal waste sites.“This government is taking decisive action to stop waste crime, putting more officers on the frontline and using drones to find the thugs behind these atrocious sites,” Hardy said.She also issued a warning to those involved in illegal dumping, saying: “My message to waste criminals is clear: there is nowhere to hide.”Under the plans outlined by the government, people caught dumping waste illegally are set to face fines of up to £5,000, compared with the current maximum of £300.More serious offences can already lead to prosecution and imprisonment. The government also plans to give the Environment Agency wider powers to confiscate money, vehicles, houses and other assets acquired through waste crime. New powers under the Crime and Policing Act 2026 are intended to speed up the process of securing confiscation orders.Illegal waste crime costs the UK more than £1 billion a yearThe incident in Birstall is part of a wider problem facing England. According to the Environment Agency's waste crime hub, illegal waste activity costs the UK more than £1 billion every year, with around 700 known illegal waste sites across England.While many of these sites are considered lower risk, the agency warns that organised criminal groups can operate on a much larger scale. Some acquire land or warehouses and fill them with thousands of tonnes of waste within weeks.The figures from 2024/25 show the scale of enforcement efforts. The Environment Agency and its partners stopped 743 illegal waste sites operating without permits and responded to 203 illegal dumping incidents. The Joint Unit for Waste Crime also led 37 operations, resulting in 40 arrests.Over the three years to March 2025, the agency recorded 211 prosecutions, which resulted in £640,000 in fines and 20 custodial sentences.However, the agency believes the problem is much bigger than the number of reported cases suggests. Only around 27 per cent of waste crimes are reported, while industry estimates suggest that as much as 20 per cent of waste could be handled illegally at some point in the supply chain.Environment Agency steps up action with intelligence and dronesTo tackle the problem, the Environment Agency is increasing its enforcement work under a 10-point plan. One of the measures involves working with Crimestoppers to share heat maps showing reported waste crime.The agency is also setting up an Operational Waste Intelligence and Analysis Unit. The team will bring together intelligence, imagery, financial information and criminal data to identify potential risks and help investigators act earlier.Where there is sufficient evidence, the agency also plans to name illegal waste sites as part of its efforts to expose those involved.What residents and landowners should knowThe Environment Agency is also urging householders to be careful when arranging for someone to remove their rubbish. People should check the public register of waste carriers before paying anyone to take waste away. If a person or business is not registered, they may be operating illegally.Landowners have also been advised to inspect vacant land and buildings regularly, as they can be held responsible for illegal waste dumped on their property.The agency's guidance is particularly important because dealing with dumped rubbish can create legal complications. Landowners should seek appropriate advice before attempting to remove waste themselves.For now, the Birstall investigation remains open. The agency has not confirmed who brought the estimated 1,000 tonnes of shredded waste to Bankwood Way, when it arrived or how much its removal will cost.Anyone with information about the incident is being urged to contact Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or the Environment Agency's incident hotline on 0800 807060.You use AI every day. articles.title: A British television director was searching for an unidentified Melbourne family seen in a forgotten 1965 film; a Sydney medical student recognised five relatives after spotting the footage on social media
articles.summary: A forgotten film shot in Melbourne in 1965 has helped reunite a Sydney medical student with relatives he did not know were in the video.
articles.body: A forgotten film shot in Melbourne in 1965 has helped reunite a Sydney medical student with relatives he did not know were in the video. The find solved a mystery for a British television director who had been looking for the family. The discovery happened after the unknown people appeared in a clip shared on social media. The student spotted five members of his own family in the video.Sydney medical student solves mystery of 1965 Melbourne family filmA forgotten film shot in Melbourne in 1965 has helped reunite a Sydney medical student with relatives he did not know were in the video. The find solved a mystery for a British television director who had been looking for the family. Zac de Boeck spotted five members of his family after his mother sent him a short video shared by ABC Melbourne on social media. The clip had sat among old film reels for decades. It showed three generations of his relatives outside their home in the Melbourne suburb of Mitcham.The find ended a global search led by British television director Karen Walsh. She had been trying to find out who the strangers were after her late father, Arthur Howes, filmed them during a trip to Australia in 1965. According to ABC News, Howes filmed the family while travelling around Australia as he thought about moving there with his young family. He later went back to England with film of Melbourne, Sydney and Perth, and never moved to Australia for good. More than 60 years later, his daughter found the unknown family in one of the old recordings and set out to learn who they were.A forgotten film sparks an international searchWalsh found the clip while sorting through her father's old film reels. The video lasted less than a minute and showed a family outside a red-brick house in suburban Melbourne. Children played in the driveway while adults watched close by. An older woman, thought to be the grandmother, stood on the garden path as the family went about their day. Walsh liked the scene, but she had no idea who the people were or where the house stood. She told ABC News that the film was too special to throw away."It is an absolutely charming little piece of video," she said.She also explained why she wanted to find the people in the film."I just feel like I'm the curator of the footage. I don't feel I own it."I think the footage really belongs to the family who were being filmed."Walsh lives in Bristol and works as a television director in the UK. She had worked in radio before and knew a local talkback show could help reach people who might know the family or the house. She contacted 774 ABC Melbourne and asked the station to help identify the people in the clip. The station shared her call for help on its breakfast show and told listeners to watch the video online. The search was also discussed on ABC Melbourne's breakfast show, where hosts asked listeners to help name the family. The old clip had been shot on an 8mm camera, which was a common way to make home movies at the time.Clues in the house and drivewayOnce the appeal aired, people began looking closely at details in the short clip for clues. The look of the brick house and a green-striped garage door drew notice, as viewers tried to figure out which Melbourne suburb it might be. The green van parked in the driveway also became a key clue in the search. Chris Scane, a historian with the Volkswagen Club of Victoria, said it was a standard split-window 1962 Kombi built in Clayton, Victoria."We'll be chasing all our members to dig in their files and see if they can find this car," he said.Some viewers thought two boys jumping off the letterbox might be wearing uniforms from Xavier College. However, the school's archivist checked its records and ruled that out. The van's number plates seemed like another way to find the owners. But VicRoads could not share details about the vehicle because of privacy laws. Even with these clues, the family stayed unknown until the video reached someone who knew the people in it.Medical student recognises five relativesThe big break came when de Boeck's mother sent him the ABC Melbourne video while he was looking at social media. She wanted to know if he knew anyone in the clip. De Boeck, a Palawa man studying medicine in Sydney, quickly spotted five people. He then contacted the ABC talkback show to tell them the video showed members of his own family. The broadcaster later confirmed that the film captured three generations of his relatives. They included his grandmother, great-uncle, great-grandparents and great-great-grandmother. The family lived in Mitcham during the 1960s, while the younger children playing in the driveway are thought to be extended family members. The first person de Boeck spotted was his great-grandmother, Dorothy Vanner."As I opened the video, I initially spotted my great-grandmother, Dorothy Vanner," he said.Dorothy, a Palawa woman, died 10 years ago. She would have turned 101 in 2026. In the 1965 clip, she appears with her husband, Ron Vanner, when both were in their 40s, along with their two children. For de Boeck, seeing his great-grandmother so much younger was hard to process. He said he had only known her as an old woman because she was 70 when he was born."When I was born, great-grandma was 70, so in my brain, I only know her as an old lady," he said."Seeing her only 10 years older than I am now, it was just mind-boggling."A rare glimpse of family historyThe clip also gave de Boeck's grandmother, Kathryn Holland, a surprise chance to see her family as they looked more than 60 years ago. Holland is the older girl standing near her parents in the driveway. She does not remember the day the film was shot or the visitor behind the camera, Arthur Howes. Even though she has many family photos, she had never seen moving video of her childhood. The old film let her watch her late mother, father and grandmother in a way that still photos could not show."I've got lots of photos, but I haven't seen them on film. It was quite a surprise," she said."I look so young!"Holland was also amazed that Walsh, a stranger living in another country, had taken the time to track down the family and return the clip to them."I just think she's extra special, going to all this trouble to find out who it belongs to," she said of Walsh."It's fabulous."For Walsh, finding the family was something she had not expected when she first called the radio station. She admitted she had almost thrown the old film away while going through her father's things."I had no faith," she said."You know, I was so close to putting the film in the bin when I was going through the footage."Something made me stop and go, 'You know what, let's just see if we can find who this is.'"The search took about 10 days from the first radio appeal to the discovery, according to ABC Melbourne's radio coverage.You use AI every day. articles.title: High-profile Colorado attorney who set own house on fire and apologized to wife and children for domestic violence dies of accidental drug overdose
articles.summary: A Colorado attorney who was accused of setting fire to his own home has died from an accidental drug overdose, months after pleading guilty to misdemeanor
articles.body: A Colorado attorney who was accused of setting fire to his own home has died from an accidental drug overdose, months after pleading guilty to misdemeanor charges involving his wife. The fire incident took place in 2025 and grabbed headlines as the attorney at that time was dealing with a high-profile case from which he had to step away.Robert Werking, 60, died in October from an accidental overdose involving fentanyl, cocaine and methamphetamine, according to the Douglas County Coroner's Office.Werking had attracted attention in July 2025 after first responders found him sitting on the front porch of his burning home in Centennial, Colorado. At the time, he was part of the legal team representing Aurora dentist James Craig, who was accused of poisoning his wife, Angela Craig, to death.The attorney's death came months after he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance and harassing his wife, Lisa Fine Moses, in an incident involving domestic violence.On June 28, 2025, when firefighters responded to a blaze at his home, they found him sitting on the porch while flames engulfed the house behind him. Investigators found evidence that an accelerant had been used to start the fire.Werking was arrested and charged with felony arson. He withdrew from Craig's defence shortly afterwards, just days before the high-profile murder trial was scheduled to begin. His wife Fine Moses was also representing the dentist. Craig was eventually convicted of first-degree murder in July 2025 and sentenced to life in prison for killing his wife.Pleaded guilty to firearm and harassment chargesWerking's legal troubles also involved a separate incident involving his wife. On March 5, 2026, he pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance and harassing Fine Moses in an act of domestic violence on June 14, 2025. The felony arson charges relating to the June 28 fire were dismissed in the interests of justice.During the sentencing hearing, Werking's attorney, David Beller, said his client had experienced mental health problems that were either undiagnosed or self-medicated. Beller said Werking had entered an inpatient treatment facility immediately after his release from jail and had made progress. Werking's law licence was also inactive because of disability. Senior Judge Dinsmore Tuttle sentenced him to one year of probation, requiring him to undergo mental health and substance-use treatment and complete 40 hours of community service.During the sentencing hearing, Werking delivered an emotional statement apologising to his family for his actions. He described Fine Moses as a "saint" and said he hoped to make things right through community service. "My actions in this case devastated my family," he said. "I hurt our family, our children so badly... I am very sorry. My actions were selfish; my actions were terrible. ...I am ashamed and I will carry this guilt and shame for the rest of my life."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: xQc lowers GTA 6 rating from 9 to 7.8, blames bugs and performance issues without Veyra
articles.summary: Twitch and Kick streamer Felix “xQc” Lengyel has rated Grand Theft Auto 6 a 7.8 out of 10, saying the game still has problems that affected his experience.
articles.body: Twitch and Kick streamer Felix “xQc” Lengyel has rated Grand Theft Auto 6 a 7.8 out of 10, saying the game still has problems that affected his experience. The rating came after he completed his first playthrough on November 22, 2026, following 62 hours with the game. However, xQc had earlier given GTA 6 a 9 out of 10 when he was using an open-source tool called Veyra. He also shared concerns about the main story, saying its early acts moved too slowly for him. His comments came during a livestream as he looked back.Felix “xQc” Lengyel Explains Why He Gave GTA 6 Two Different RatingsxQc first spoke about his score around the ten-hour point of his broadcast. At that stage, he was impressed enough to rate GTA 6 as high as 9.1. He then settled on 9.0 but made it clear that the score depended on a tool he was using while playing.The streamer was referring to Veyra, an open-source tool that uses AI frame generation. According to xQc, it made the game more enjoyable and improved the way it looked and ran on his setup. He said GTA 6 would receive a much lower score without it.“Without this program, this game is a solid ******* 7.8. It is what it is,” xQc said during the stream.He later explained that the game still had bugs and performance problems. He also pointed to work that was still being done to improve its visuals. In his view, these issues kept the current experience from earning a higher score.xQc added that a future PC release could change his opinion. He suggested that the game might score above nine if its technical problems were addressed and its performance improved. However, he did not give a separate confirmed score for a PC version. His 7.8 rating was his assessment of the game without Veyra, while the 9.0 score reflected his experience with the tool.The ratings reflected two different playing conditions, with Veyra playing a major part in his higher score.Felix “xQc” Lengyel Says GTA 6’s Early Story Acts Felt SlowThe streamer also spoke about the game's main story and said its pace left him disappointed. He felt GTA 6 had plenty of interesting stories outside the central plot, especially when players took time to explore rather than focus only on the next mission.xQc compared the experience with earlier Grand Theft Auto games. He said the game could feel “fantastic” when players set aside expectations about how quickly the main story should move. But he warned that anyone expecting a steady pace from the main plot might not enjoy the opening sections as much.“I mean, I know I was,” he said while explaining that he had felt disappointed by the pacing. He described acts one through three-and-a-half as “very slow and clunky.”His comments were about the way the story unfolded, rather than a claim that the game had nothing else to offer. In fact, he praised the amount of other stories available to players. His point was that the wider world and side content could hold his interest, even when the main storyline did not move at the speed he wanted.xQc is not the only streamer to share a mixed reaction to GTA 6’s story. Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” also discussed the game after completing it and gave its story a 6.5 out of 10. Lacy’s score focused on the story, while xQc discussed both the overall game experience and its pacing.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
